keep: The idea is named in one line up front and the closing takeaway is all bold and footnoted to [^1][^2], whose quotes support it.

The why is complete: the whole is fixed, cutting shares it, so more pieces sharing one unchanged whole means less for each; the worked example (1000 ÷ 5 = 200 mm, 1000 ÷ 10 = 100 mm) is computed from the stated rule.

The misconception (1/5 > 1/2 because 5 > 2, [^3][^4]) is shown failing: ten tenths longer than 200 mm would make more than 2000 mm from one metre. It is not called wrong in general: 10 pieces are more pieces than 5.
The brief names the cause (raising the number of equal pieces) and the effect (every piece on the bar shrinks, 200 mm to 100 mm), one control, outputs computable from length = 1000 ÷ pieces.
Names match i1 and i2: bottom number, top number, the whole, the 1000 mm metre, the label '1/5 of the metre'. Only one new term, [[unit fraction]], used again in practice.
Every [^n] is a listed source on words its quote supports; sources lists exactly those cited.
fix: Padding: the second readout 'Drop with one more piece' brings its own rule (1000 ÷ n − 1000 ÷ (n + 1)), a third paragraph in whatAmILookingAt, half of explain's fifth paragraph, a rule-of-thumb sentence and a practice bullet. The one thing is the piece shrinking; the plot already shows the shape. Keep one readout, and say in one or two sentences why the curve flattens and never reaches zero.
Talking about the lesson instead of teaching: 'Hold on to that claim, because this lesson is about what happens to…' and 'Here is the habit this lesson is built to break'. Cut or shorten.

Shape: the rule should be stated in words before the worked example, as the recommended template says; the draft puts the bold rule after the example. Link the rule to i2's fit test (whole ÷ piece = count) turned round (whole ÷ count = piece), so the earlier lesson's name is reused.

Analogy breaks: 'a filament lamp's resistance changes with its temperature, so real identical lamps share a little unevenly' is muddled (matching lamps in series carry the same current and run alike; unevenness comes from real lamps not being perfectly matched). Say that plainly. 'Each gets the full 230 V however many you add' in parallel is an ideal-supply claim: 'near enough the full 230 V'. Word 230 V as a chosen example ('say a 230 V supply').
False absolute in practice: 'The size of one piece is always the whole divided by the bottom number' holds only for equal pieces; drop 'always' and keep the condition.
'for unit fractions this is the whole story of comparing them' needs 'of one whole', since comparison is valid only for the same whole [^11].

numbers must match what is shown once the second readout goes: drop the five 'drop' entries except the two the explanation still uses (1 to 2 pieces: 500 mm; 10 to 11 pieces: 9.1 mm), kept as computed.
The practice mistake about the shrinking being front-loaded uses 166.7 (2 to 3 pieces), a number nothing else shows; use the same 500 and 9.1 as the explanation and the numbers list.
